sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 1 어, 저 사람 좋은 사람 아니었어?
sents: “Perception is everything.”
This famous saying shows the importance of image in contemporary society.
This is why public figures are always on the lookout for new ways to win the public’s approval.
One clever trick they use is called “funwashing”, which refers to the act of concealing unpleasant truths using a favorable image.
Funwashing typically involves prominent individuals participating in silly and entertaining public events.
Their goal is to appear likable and easygoing.
For example, a controversial politician might join a televised dance competition.
Through the display of smiling and dancing awkwardly in stylish attire, the politician effectively projects a significantly more lighthearted persona.
While this practice may seem harmless at first glance, it actually hurts society by distracting the public from these figures’ problematic actions.
People focus on their entertaining personas rather than their flaws.
Subsequently, they do not face any consequences for the problems they cause and may even commit worse misconduct later.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 2 데이터, 어디까지 빚어봤니?
sents: For centuries, artists have relied on physical materials such as paint, stone, or metal to create their work.
In recent years, however, a new question has emerged: What if data itself became an artistic medium?
This question lies at the heart of the work of Turkish artist Refik Anadol.
Anadol is known for using artificial intelligence to transform large sets of data into immersive visual experiences.
Instead of painting canvases, he designs systems that process images, sounds, and recordings through machine-learning models.
The results are not static paintings but constantly shifting forms that resemble moving sculptures made of light.
What makes this approach unusual is the role of data.
Traditionally, data is used to analyze or explain reality.
In Anadol’s work, however, data is treated as a raw material, similar to clay or paint.
For example, thousands of archived images can be fed into an AI model, which then produces new visual patterns no single human could design alone.
The artwork does not simply display information; it reimagines it.
This approach challenges common ideas about creativity.
If a machine can generate visual forms, where does authorship begin and end?
Anadol argues that creativity still comes from human choices—deciding which data to use, how to train the model, and how the final work is presented.
In this way, AI becomes a collaborator rather than a replacement.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 3 기타가 없는 기타 대회
sents: As music blasts from the speakers, a performer rocks out on stage, jamming on his guitar.
However, when you look closer, you realize that he’s not playing an instrument—he’s playing air!
Welcome to the Air Guitar World Championships!
This unique event originated in 1996 as a small contest.
That first competition was a hit, so it has been held in Finland every year since.
During the competition, participants execute their air guitar routines in two 60-second rounds.
Evaluation criteria for determining the winner are originality, stage presence, technical ability, and artistic impression.
To get a better score, contestants often wear outlandish costumes and showcase their impressive air guitar skills to entertain the audience.
They sometimes even jump into the crowd!
Although it may look a bit silly, the event actually has a noble objective of pursuing inclusivity and peace.
Fundamentally, playing air guitar requires no specific skills or equipment.
This lowers the barriers to participation, making the contest accessible to people of all ages and backgrounds.
Moreover, as its slogan “Make Air Not War” suggests, this witty event fosters global unity through the universal language of music.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 4 He, She... Why Not Both?
sents: If you think color-changing chameleons are nature’s greatest masters of disguise, think again.
Hammer corals, especially a species called Fimbriaphyllia ancora, are performing more incredible magic: they change their gender.
In Nanwan Bay, Taiwan, these creatures form large communities called colonies.
What makes them extraordinary is their unique ability to transform their gender as a group.
In 2011, marine biologists observed that about 70 percent of F. ancora colonies underwent a synchronized switch from female to male!
Even more remarkable was that this wasn’t a one-time event.
These same groups continued this cycle, alternating between female and male year after year.
The discovery has drawn scientific attention, leading to research into the underlying causes.
Scientists believe that there are two reasons for this phenomenon.
First, it significantly increases the likelihood of reproduction occurring.
For example, mating between two primarily female colonies becomes possible when many members of one colony change their gender to male.
Second, this reproductive advantage also leads to much greater genetic diversity.
Corals that periodically change their gender have access to a wider range of mates, resulting in more varied combinations of partners.
The remarkable flexibility of these corals serves as a quiet reminder that survival often lies in the ability to change.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 1 100년째 마르지 않는 지갑의 비밀
sents: For her profound impact on the literary world, Korean author Han Kang was awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize for Literature.
Along with the prestigious gold medal, she received prize money exceeding one million dollars (11 million Swedish kronor).
But how can such substantial rewards be awarded to multiple winners across different categories?
It all dates back to Alfred Nobel, the Swedish scientist who made his fortune largely from inventing dynamite.
Before his death in 1896, Nobel directed that the profits from his substantial fortune be invested.
These funds would be used to honor groundbreaking contributions in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace.
The first prizes, awarded in 1901, were worth about $1 million by today’s standards.
Over the years, the prize amounts have fluctuated depending on global events and Swedish currency values.
For example, in 1919, right after World War I, the prize dipped to a mere $230,000 in today’s terms and didn’t recover its initial value until 1991.
Currently, thanks to smart investments, Nobel’s trust has grown to an impressive $500 million.
This ensures substantial prize amounts and financial stability for decades to come.
Perhaps this is the lasting legacy of Nobel, a man who was troubled by the destructive impact of dynamite and sought to leave behind something meaningful for humanity.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 2 무서운 게 약이 된다
sents: You may think that horror films merely make for a thrilling experience, but recent research shows that they also reduce anxiety.
Psychologists who have examined the effects that scary movies have on the psyche believe that horror films allow viewers to have a controlled experience of fear.
From an evolutionary perspective, fear evolved to protect us from possible harm by provoking strong reactions such as a racing heart or an urge to escape.
When people watch scary movies, their brains and bodies react as if they are in danger.
However, their minds are comfortable in the knowledge that the environment is safe and predictable.
This allows them to explore feelings of anxiety without risk, which ultimately helps them understand and manage their own stress.
Psychologists also suggest that horror films help the brain become accustomed to uncertainty.
By exposing ourselves to fear in a controlled manner, we can improve how our minds predict and cope with real-life challenges.
In this sense, watching horror movies is a kind of emotional rehearsal.
Overall, rather than simply causing stress, horror films may help people deal with anxieties.
They offer a means to face fears safely, test psychological limits, and increase emotional resilience.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 3 빙산의 일각? 아니, 화산의 일각!
sents: When you think of a volcano, you probably envision a towering mountain spewing dense clouds of smoke and ash up into the sky.
Yet surprisingly, about 80 percent of all volcanic eruptions actually occur in the ocean!
Much like their counterparts on land, underwater volcanoes result from the accumulation of gases and molten rock deep in the earth.
These gradually rise up to the surface until they burst out through vents.
But an underwater eruption is generally much less violent than a land one.
The extreme pressure generated by the seawater above the vent compresses the released gases, robbing them of much of their explosive force.
At the same time, the molten rock—called lava—cools and hardens much more quickly in water.
The resulting rock formations may take the form of car-sized lumps that resemble giant fluffy pillows or flat, circular sheets that spread out evenly in every direction.
One noteworthy effect of this process is the creation of a seamount.
As each new layer of lava hardens on top of the previous one, that section of the seafloor gradually rises.
Eventually, it can rise above the surface of the water as an island.
One of the most famous examples of this process is the islands of Hawaii.
Each was created as a result of an underwater volcano eruption, and a new seamount named Loihi is in the process of being formed.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 4 No Rules, No School, No Problem
sents: What does it take to become a great artist?
Studying at an art school?
Correct, but that’s not the only way.
In fact, many celebrated paintings have been created by people who never followed the conventional path!
Collectively referred to as naïve art, these works are known for their childlike simplicity.
They feature bright, vibrant colors and do not follow traditional rules of perspective.
Most notably, objects in the foreground and background are often the same size and depicted with the same level of detail.
By rejecting the conventions of mainstream art, creators of naïve art are able to focus on expressing their feelings.
Perhaps the most representative figure of the naïve art movement was the 19th-century French artist Henri Rousseau.
Although he worked as a customs officer for over 20 years, he held the dream of painting throughout his career.
He taught himself how to paint in imaginative ways, including by copying diverse pieces displayed in the Louvre Museum.
Today, creators of naïve art like Rousseau are widely praised for their intuitive form of expression.
They prove that creativity can make up for a lack of training when it comes to creating great works of art.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 1 ‘비행(Flight)’이 ‘비행(Misdeed)’인 시대
sents: Whether it’s for a business trip or an overseas vacation, air travel has become a common feature of modern life.
At the same time, however, a growing number of voices are pushing back against frequent flying.
One such form of criticism is flygskam, which means “flight shame” in Swedish.
The movement originated in 2018, when Swedish climate activists declared they would no longer fly unless necessary due to concerns about the harmful effects of rising emissions from airplanes.
A UN study warns that the aviation industry will become one of the largest emitters of CO2 by 2050 unless concrete steps are taken to prevent this.

So far, thanks to the flight shame movement, almost 40 percent of Swedes now say they choose to take trains instead of flights when possible, and the number of passengers at domestic airports has dropped by 15 percent.
Activists like Greta Thunberg are helping to spread this movement beyond Sweden.
In 2019, she brought attention to the environmental harm of flying when she traveled by boat from the United Kingdom to New York to speak at a climate conference.
While critics note that individual actions alone cannot halt global warming, flygskam demonstrates how personal choices, when adopted widely, create measurable industry changes.
The movement has already raised public awareness and will hopefully continue to accelerate effective responses to the ecological crisis.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 2 책 읽다가 국경을 넘었다
sents: Streets usually connect different parts of a city, but this is not always the case in an American town called Derby Line.
Residents of this town need to be careful because if they take the wrong street, they may suddenly find themselves in Canada!
Founded in 1791, Derby Line is situated in northern Vermont right at the border between Canada and the United States.
There, it joins with the Canadian town of Stanstead, which has existed since 1796.
For many years, these two towns functioned as one community, with residents crossing the border easily to visit friends, go shopping, or take a walk.
But since the terrorist attacks of 9/11, this has no longer been possible due to the implementation of stricter border controls.
A person crossing anywhere other than at an official checkpoint is detected by cameras, triggering a response by border guards.
Fortunately, residents of both towns can still interact freely in the Haskell Free Library and Opera House, which was intentionally constructed on the border in 1904.
There is an entrance from each country, and visitors can move around freely within.
A line on the floor of the library area even marks the border, so a visitor can read a book in two countries at once!

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 3 뼈는 없어도 썰은 넘쳐나요~
sents: From the tentacled Kraken, said to drag ships beneath the ocean, to Bigfoot, an ape-like creature rumored to roam remote forests, stories of mysterious animals have captured humanity’s attention for centuries.
No clear scientific evidence has proved their existence yet, but their long history in human culture raises an interesting question: What if some legendary animals are more than just myths?
This question led to the development of cryptozoology, a field that searches for mysterious creatures around the world and tries to confirm their existence.
The term was popularized in the mid-20th century by Bernard Heuvelmans, a Belgian-French zoologist often called the “father of cryptozoology.”
He believed that careful analysis of historical records, local legends, and eyewitness reports might point to undiscovered species.
In this sense, cryptozoology sits at the crossroads of zoology, anthropology, and folklore.
However, cryptozoology has long faced serious criticism.
Most scientists argue that it lacks reliable evidence and does not follow strict scientific methods.
Sightings are often based on personal testimony rather than repeatable experiments, and physical proof—such as bones or living specimens—is usually missing.
As a result, cryptozoology is generally not recognized as a legitimate scientific discipline.
Even so, the influence of cryptozoology cannot be dismissed.
It reflects a deep human desire to believe that the natural world still holds untold secrets.
By exploring the boundaries between the known and the unknown, cryptozoology has inspired countless novels, films, and fantasy worlds.
More than a quest for hidden animals, it reveals humanity’s appetite for mystery endures.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 4 You Shall Not Pass!
sents: With one second remaining in a basketball game, Stephen Curry gets a chance for a final shot.
Yet no defender rushes to guard the league’s greatest shooter.
How did he get so open?
It was thanks to one of the sport’s best strategies: the elevator screen.
While a typical screen play involves a single screener blocking a defender to create space for a shooter, the elevator screen is highly effective because it uses two screeners to assist the shooter.
The screeners position themselves close together, creating a corridor for the shooter to run through.
As the shooter cuts between them to receive the pass, the screeners quickly close the gap—like elevator doors slamming shut—preventing defenders from following the shooter.
This seemingly simple movement demands precise execution from all participants.
First, the attacking players should disguise the play so the opposing defenders can’t prepare for it.
Then, the screeners must close the gap at the exact moment to seal off defenders while avoiding offensive fouls.
The pass has to be delivered right on time—after the shooter is open and before the defenders get past the screeners.
And finally, the shooter has to score!

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 1 새똥 때문에 전쟁까지 일어났다고?
sents: You wouldn’t be happy if a bird pooped on your head.
But in the 1800s, you might have felt differently.
At the time, so many people wanted bird poop, or guano, that nations even fought wars over it.
Why was guano in such high demand back then?
Guano contains high levels of nitrogen, which is essential for plant growth.
During the 19th century, Western nations struggled to increase soil productivity to feed rapidly growing populations.
As a result, nitrogen-rich resources became extremely valuable.
In the eyes of European nations, the Chincha Islands of Peru came to be seen as a treasure trove.
The Chincha Islands were uniquely suited to meet this demand.
Seabirds there had an abundant supply of fish, producing massive amounts of guano.
At the same time, the islands’ arid climate meant there was little rain to wash these deposits away, allowing guano to accumulate in layers as deep as 60 meters.
This natural resource gained international attention when guano samples were brought to Europe by Alexander von Humboldt, a German naturalist and explorer.
However, guano’s scarcity made it difficult to obtain in large quantities.

As its value increased, competition for control of guano-rich regions intensified, eventually leading to armed conflicts such as the Chincha Islands War of 1865 between Spain, Peru, and other South American nations.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 2 부먹파도 찍어 먹는다는 ‘이것’
sents: Which do you prefer, pouring sauce over food or dipping food in it?
If you prefer the latter, you will enjoy dips because they are thick sauces that are made for dipping food in.
A well-known example is hummus, a thick, creamy dip made from chickpeas.
It originated in the Middle East, with early recipes dating back to the 13th century.
Although hummus is sometimes eaten on its own, it is most commonly scooped up with other foods.
Nowadays, many people around the world enjoy hummus.
The primary reason behind its widespread popularity is its simple preparation method!
Here is a recipe.
Why don’t you try it yourself?
Boil chickpeas in water until soft.
Put the boiled chickpeas in a blender after draining the water.
Add olive oil, salt, minced garlic, and lemon juice.
Blend the ingredients until you have a smooth and creamy mixture.
It’s a piece of cake, isn’t it?
Now, enjoy your homemade hummus by dipping vegetables or bread into it!

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 3 거절로 만든 최초의 열쇠
sents: “Every no takes me closer to a yes.”
This famous quote is by Bessie Coleman, the first African-American female pilot.
She spent her whole life trying to get people to say yes.
Born in 1892, Coleman worked as a manicurist during World War I.
As a Black woman in the US, her job opportunities were limited to service roles.
It wasn’t until her brother returned from the war and spoke about the female pilots in France that everything changed.
She admired their achievements and developed a new ambition—to become a pilot!
But she was rejected from flight schools in the US due to both her race and gender.
Thus, she went to France!
This was a courageous decision, as it involved not only a long journey to France, but also the challenge of learning French.
Despite the obstacles, Coleman earned her pilot’s license in 1921 and gained international recognition as a skilled aviator.
A few months later, she returned to the US with a determination to enter the aviation industry.
She started performing in air shows as a stunt pilot.
In addition, as an activist, Coleman encouraged African Americans to become pilots, raising funds to establish a flight school to train Black aviators.
Her efforts opened doors for hopeful Black pilots!

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 4 Just a Dot. Just Everything.
sents: A faint beam of light stretches across the darkness of space.
Inside it, a tiny blue dot appears—easy to overlook, almost insignificant.
Yet that small dot is Earth, the home of every human who has ever lived.
This image was taken on February 14, 1990, by the spacecraft Voyager 1.
Having completed most of its assigned mission, Voyager 1 was preparing to pass beyond the solar system.
Before leaving the solar system, scientists at NASA decided to turn the camera back toward the inner planets and take one final photograph of Earth.
The decision carried risks.
Even from a great distance, pointing a camera toward the Sun could damage the spacecraft’s instruments.
After careful adjustments were made, the photograph was taken.
When the image was captured, sunlight scattered inside the camera lens, creating the pale beam seen in the photograph.
By chance, Earth fell within that beam, and the light made our planet appear even more trivial—almost lost within the vast darkness of space.
Reflecting on this image, American astronomer Carl Sagan described it as a humbling self-portrait of humanity and its existence.
From nearly six billion kilometers away, everything humans have ever accomplished—every civilization, conflict, and dream—appears reduced to a single, tiny point.
It was from this perspective that Sagan gave that small and ordinary-looking dot its name: the Pale Blue Dot.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 1 슬라임 벼락을 맞는 시상식이 있다?!
sents: “This year’s Favorite Movie Actor winner, Robert Downey Jr.!”
Hearing his name, he excitedly comes up on stage to accept his award.
Then out of nowhere, a massive amount of neon green slime covers him!
Surprisingly, it’s a common scene at the Kids’ Choice Awards.
Since 1987, the Kids’ Choice Awards has been presented every year by Nickelodeon, a children’s TV network in the US.
The awards show honors winners for various categories, ranging from favorite TV show and video game to most beloved social media influencer and villain character.
As its name suggests, the winners of the awards are chosen by kids through online voting.
Instead of receiving a typical golden trophy, the winners get an orange blimp with “Nickelodeon” written on it.
Without a doubt, the most distinctive feature of this awards show is the neon green slime.
It was first used in the early ’80s to add a new twist to TV programs on Nickelodeon.
As these scenes gained popularity, it became an iconic element of the network.
Award winners and even hosts can get covered with it at any moment, adding more fun and excitement to the awards.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 2 도심 속 빈 땅에 씨앗 폭탄을 던져라!
sents: Who planted sunflowers next to this busy street?
And who put flower boxes in the windows of an abandoned building?
It’s the work of guerrilla gardeners!
Guerrilla gardeners are individuals or small groups who engage in unauthorized gardening, often transforming neglected urban areas into green spaces.
The practice began as a form of protest against urban decay in the 1970s.
For example, in New York City, a group called the Green Guerillas began throwing seed bombs—mixtures of seeds and clay—into vacant lots to transform them into gardens.
In 1974, their efforts were acknowledged by the city government, which agreed to rent them a large lot for the sum of $1 per month.
This site became the Liz Christy Community Garden, taking its name from one of the group’s founders.
It still exists today as the oldest community garden in the city.
In fact, it has inspired hundreds of similar community garden projects across New York City over the past five decades.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 3 닿지도 않았는데 왜 끌려요?
sents: If you rub a balloon back and forth across your head, your hair will stick to the balloon.
Have you ever wondered why?
Most objects have the same number of positive and negative charges.
But when two objects are rubbed together, negatively charged particles called electrons move from one to the other.
If this results in an imbalance between positively and negatively charged particles on the objects, static electricity is produced.
For example, when you rub the balloon against your hair, electrons move from your hair to the balloon, giving it a negative charge and your hair a positive charge.
As opposite charges attract, your hair sticks to the balloon.
Here’s a fun way to witness static electricity in action.
First, rub a plastic ruler with a wool cloth for several seconds, then slowly bring it near small bits of paper scattered on a table.
You’ll see the paper pieces jump up and stick to the ruler.
This happens because rubbing the ruler gives it extra electrons, making it negatively charged.
When the charged ruler comes close to the paper, which doesn’t carry a charge of its own, the positive parts inside the paper move closer, so the paper is pulled toward the ruler.
This shows how static electricity can make objects move without touching them.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 4 Every History Book Has an Author.
sents: Cabaret Crusades, a series of three Arabic-language films created by Egyptian artist Wael Shawky, is unlike any collection of war movies you’ve seen before.
The films depict the Crusades, when European Christians battled Muslims for control of Jerusalem between 1095 and 1291.
Instead of human actors, the scenes in these films are performed by puppets, some with animal characteristics like cat ears or the long neck and teeth of camels.
These films highlight common themes in Shawky’s work, one of which is that there is no single perspective on the past.
While the European version of the Crusades is the most widely known, it is only one interpretation, not the definitive one.
By providing an alternate viewpoint through the lens of Arab historians, Shawky prompts viewers to consider a different perspective when evaluating history.
The movies also bring attention to the ambiguity between facts and fiction.
According to Shawky, history is not completely based on objective facts.
Puppets represent this idea, since their strings symbolize manipulation.
Just as the puppets can be controlled by outside forces, history can be shaped by those who tell it.
These themes urge viewers to question the objectivity of familiar historical narratives.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 1 내 기억이 가짜라고?
sents: Misremembering something is a fairly common experience.
But you would probably be shocked to learn that thousands of other people share the same false memory.
This phenomenon is known as the Mandela effect.
It is named after Nelson Mandela, who was the president of South Africa from 1994 to 1999.
Although Mandela died in 2013, a large number of people remember him passing away in the 1980s while still in prison.
This is the most famous example of the Mandela effect, but there are many others.
For instance, some people recall a movie called Shazaam starring the comedian Sinbad, even though no such film was ever made.
The reason this happens is that we tend to fill in missing information with incorrect or unrelated details.
In the case of Nelson Mandela, his long imprisonment and the limited media coverage during this period may have contributed to confusion about his fate.
In addition, a film portrayed the death of another human rights activist in prison, and this may have influenced people’s memories of Mandela’s life.
This led many to falsely remember that he had died while imprisoned, even though he was later released and went on to become president.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 2 식은 밥이 사람 잡아요!
sents: You might think it’s fine to eat cooked rice that’s been sitting on the counter for a while.
After all, what harm could it do?
But it’s better to be safe than sorry.
Some leftovers can be far more dangerous than they appear, and in extreme cases, they can even be deadly.
In 2008, a 20-year-old student died after eating food that had been left on his kitchen counter for five days.
It turned out that he had succumbed to “fried rice syndrome,” a type of food poisoning caused by a bacterium called Bacillus cereus.
Commonly found in uncooked rice, the bacterium itself is harmless, but its spores aren’t.
They can multiply and produce a deadly toxin if they’re heated and then left in the temperature “danger zone” of 4 to 60 degrees Celsius for too long.
Even reheating the food won’t eliminate the problem because the spores are capable of tolerating high heat.
According to experts, cooked rice shouldn’t be left at room temperature for more than two hours—and it’s not just rice that you need to be wary of.
Other carbohydrate-rich foods like pasta, potatoes, and beans can cause fried rice syndrome, too!

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 3 표절이 아니라 절한 거야~
sents: You’re watching a movie where a boy is given a puppy and lifts it high in the air.
Wait a minute, this looks familiar.
It’s reminiscent of the scene from The Lion King!
Some might say it’s plagiarism—completely stealing from another work without credit to the original creator.
However, it’s actually an homage commonly seen in movies.
It is an artistic technique where creators show respect to previous works by intentionally referencing iconic moments.
For a scene to be considered an homage, it should be a transparent reference, and it should involve a slight change from the original.
For instance, in the movie Toy Story 2, a globe comes loose and rolls after Buzz Lightyear.
This moment is an homage to an Indiana Jones movie, where the main character escapes a huge rolling rock.
Such homages can serve as little gifts for audiences who recognize the reference.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 4 The Paycheck-to-Paycheck Paradox
sents: “Henry!”
When the name echoed through the room, dozens of heads turned.
It’s a pretty common name, after all.
But even if your name isn’t Henry, you can still be a HENRY.
That’s because HENRY is also an acronym that stands for “High Earners, Not Rich Yet!”
This acronym was invented in the early 2000s to describe a group of Americans with high-paying jobs who have not yet accumulated significant wealth.
Today, it is commonly used by marketing professionals to describe a specific group of consumers.
In general, HENRYs are highly educated people who are early in their careers.
While monthly budgets can be large, most of them are eaten up by expenses such as student debt or rent.

Furthermore, as many of them live in high-cost cities like New York, where professionals are socially expected to maintain expensive lifestyles, they live paycheck to paycheck, leaving no room to save or invest in assets like stocks and real estate.
Still, due to their high incomes and willingness to spend on luxury goods and services to maintain their lifestyles, HENRYs are attractive targets for marketers.
Provided they can keep their debt under control, continue their careers, and build up their savings, these individuals will probably be wealthy one day, even if they aren’t today.
In the end, companies that win them early may benefit as their earnings and spending power continue to grow over time.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 1 하늘의 별 딸래, 체조에서 만점 딸래
sents: In 1976, Nadia Comaneci received the first perfect score in gymnastics.
With this achievement, the 14-year-old Romanian gymnast made Olympic history!
Under the scoring system applied to Comaneci, gymnasts were awarded a single score out of 10 based on how well their routine was executed.
This system encouraged gymnasts to play it safe.
Those who completed easier routines cleanly got higher scores, while those who performed complicated routines with minor errors received lower scores.
The International Gymnastics Federation addressed this problem in 2006 by changing the scoring system.
Gymnasts still receive an execution score out of 10, but they also get a difficulty score that does not have a limit.
A perfect score is now impossible to achieve!
Some people have criticized the new system because it is harder for spectators to understand what makes a strong score, whereas before, it was clear that a score of 10 was perfect.
But others say that it encourages gymnasts to innovate and take risks, which helps the sport advance.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 2 튀면 살아남는다!
sents: Look at the characters above for a few seconds, then look away.
Which one do you still remember?
If it is “COZ,” you’re experiencing the Von Restorff effect.
Also known as the isolation effect, it was first described by the German psychologist Hedwig von Restorff in 1933.
She demonstrated that when an item in a group is noticeably distinguishable from the others, it is more likely to be remembered.
The Von Restorff effect is related to how our brains are wired to gather information —when something stands out, our attention is automatically drawn to it.
And once this happens, we tend to spend more time focusing on the distinctive item than usual.
Both of these factors combine to increase the likelihood of a long-term memory being formed.
Many companies have utilized the Von Restorff effect for branding purposes.
One well-known example is Apple’s white earphones, first introduced in the early 2000s.
When most earphones were black or gray, the visual contrast of Apple’s bright white earbuds made them instantly recognizable.
This visual isolation makes the brand easily identifiable and memorable in a crowded marketplace.
Similarly, Toblerone chocolate has a distinct triangular shape, which sets it apart from conventional rectangular chocolate bars.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 3 이발사의 손에 메스가?
sents: Imagine you lived in Europe during the Middle Ages.
When you got injured, who would you go to for help?
Strange as it may seem, you would probably visit the same person that cut your hair— your barber.
In the 11th century AD, barbers in Europe treated wounds and pulled out teeth.
Why did their role expand beyond shaving clients and trimming their hair and nails?
It was because the highly educated doctors of the time refused to perform surgery, considering it a form of manual labor that was beneath their dignity.
Consequently, barbers, who skillfully used sharp instruments daily, began to provide these medical services instead of them.
As a result, barbers came to be known as barber-surgeons, and they formed organizations called guilds, with many rules to control their profession.
For example, anyone who wanted to be a barber-surgeon had to train for several years with a qualified member.

Although the modernization of medicine— beginning with a 1745 English law splitting barbers and surgeons into separate guilds— eventually eliminated the medical role of barbers, you can still see its influence today.
Most notably, the white stripe of a modern barber’s pole represents bandages, while the ones with red and blue symbolize arterial and venous blood, respectively.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 4 Being Ugly Doesn’t Mean Being Yucky
sents: According to the United Nations Environment Programme report, 19 percent of food that reaches consumers is thrown out before being used.
Moreover, 13 percent of food is lost before it even reaches consumers.
That means about one-third of all food is being wasted!
Among various reasons, one is as simple as food appearing ugly.
Activist Tristram Stuart launched the Feeding the 5000 campaign to raise awareness about this absurd problem and ultimately resolve it.
The campaign takes the form of a public event that provides meals for 5,000 people using food that would otherwise go to waste.
The first event was held in London in December 2009.
To support the event, Stuart and his colleagues partnered with local producers and received leftover food as contributions.
After food and ingredients were collected, volunteers cooked and served meals to thousands of visitors who attended the feast.
The campaign not only managed to reduce the amount of food waste but also made substantial contributions to changing negative perceptions about ugly foods.
Following this successful launch, more than 50 additional events have been held worldwide.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 1 이 책 누가 좀 읽어줄 사람...?
sents: The Rare Book Library at Yale University houses the first printed Bible and the first printed collection of Shakespeare’s plays.
However, many visitors are especially fascinated by the Voynich manuscript, considered one of history’s greatest puzzles.

Named after Wilfrid Voynich, the Polish book dealer who purchased it in Rome in 1912, the manuscript contains 240 pages written in an unknown language and adorned with bizarre, colorful illustrations.
These include depictions of unidentified plants, mysterious astronomical objects, and people in strange, unexplained settings.
Over the years, code breakers, linguists, and historians have worked to decode the manuscript.
They’ve determined that the book was made from fourteen full calfskins and had once belonged to an emperor in the sixteenth century before being lost.
Handwriting analysis suggests the manuscript was created by five different individuals, yet scholars are still uncertain about the language or meaning of the text.
A recent computer analysis showed the text might be a type of Hebrew, while another research team thought it could be an old Turkish language.
The manuscript’s possibilities continue to draw scholars eager to solve the mystery within.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 2 이 로봇, 진짜 개구리네!
sents: Most robots are made of metal or plastic, which can turn into environmental waste when they stop working.
But imagine if there were living robots made from organic material.
While this may sound like science fiction, such robots became a reality in 2020.
Using skin cells from the Xenopus laevis frog, researchers created tiny biological machines called xenobots.
Each one is about the size of a grain of sand and uses tiny hair-like structures to swim.
Unlike mechanical robots that rely on software programming, xenobots are controlled by altering their shape and size to encourage desired behaviors.

In relation to this, researchers discovered an optimal design resembling Pac-Man, a classic, ball-shaped game character with a small triangular mouth, which enables xenobots to replicate by gathering spare skin cells and forming new xenobots autonomously.
Scientists envision a hopeful future with xenobots, where they can be programmed to deliver medicine, detect cancer cells, or collect microplastics in the ocean.
In addition, once their task is done, the xenobots naturally decompose without causing any harm to the environment.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 3 거기로 안 나갈 건데?
sents: Once upon a time, a new kangaroo arrived at the Harrisburg Zoo.
Jessica, the zookeeper, immediately recognized that the lively little creature was quite playful.
To prevent this energetic jumper from causing trouble, she increased the height of the fence to five meters.
Although she had felt certain that the kangaroo could not leap over the formidable walls, she saw the young kangaroo hopping around outside as she was transporting buckets of feed the next morning.
She thought to herself, “How on earth did it get out? Never mind, I’ll just make the fence higher.”
The fence was raised to 10 meters, 15 meters, and finally 20 meters, but the kangaroo kept escaping.
At a loss, Jessica threw her hands up in despair.
A curious camel that observed all this asked the kangaroo, “How much longer can you keep this up?”
The kangaroo looked back smiling and responded, “Even if she makes the fence 1,000 meters tall, it won’t matter until she finds out the hole under the fence.”

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 4 Born to Crave Salt?
sents: Choose one: a bag of salty potato chips or a pack of sweet chocolate cookies.
If you choose the former, you might have a salt tooth!
This term refers to a strong craving for salt.
However, a salt tooth is more than a personal preference; it is influenced by biological and genetic factors!
Sodium, a key component of salt, is essential for various physical processes.
For instance, the human body requires sodium to maintain electrolyte balance and proper hydration.
When sodium levels are low, the body may trigger cravings for salty foods to restore these.
A study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition highlights how low sodium intake can lead to an increased appetite for salty snacks.
Research has also shown that certain individuals with a salt tooth have genetic predispositions that affect their taste sensitivity.
For example, variations in the SCNN1B gene have been associated with reduced salt taste sensitivity, which may in turn contribute to a preference for saltier foods.
This genetic factor can shape dietary preferences from early childhood and persist into adulthood.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 1 본캐는 명작 제조기, 부캐는 신조어 자판기?
sents: “If he swaggers, let him not come here.”
While swagger, which means “to walk or behave in a bold and often arrogant way,” may sound like a modern word, it first appeared in Shakespeare’s Henry IV, Part 2 in 1600.
This word is just one example of the many that Shakespeare introduced into English, helping the language flourish with a richer and more expressive vocabulary.
His creativity with language was reflected in his various methods of word formation.
One common technique was to combine two existing words, like cold-hearted meaning “without sympathy” or lack-luster meaning “dull.”
Another way was to convert a word’s part of speech, such as when he used the noun elbow as a verb to mean “to push aside.”
He also accomplished this by adding prefixes and suffixes, as seen when he turned the verb excite into the noun excitement by adding -ment.
He didn’t limit himself to English when introducing words either.
He borrowed terms from other languages, such as when he changed the Dutch word randten into rant, meaning “to speak in a loud or wild manner.”
So whether swaggering down the street or bone-weary with exhaustion, you can thank Shakespeare for enriching the English language.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 2 아침에 열리고 오후엔 닫히는 것은?
sents: What opens in the morning but closes in the afternoon?
This may sound like a riddle, but it’s actually a description of the petals of a morning glory!
This trumpet-shaped flower usually blooms at dawn, only to wilt by the afternoon.
This unique blooming pattern gives this plant its poetic name, morning glory.
The distinctive pattern is a result of exposure to sunlight in the morning.
These plants contain light-sensitive proteins called photoreceptors that respond to this light.
Once activated, these receptors send signals that cause water to flow into the cells of the flower buds.
As the petal cells absorb water, the internal pressure increases, making the petals swell and unfold.
By afternoon, however, warm temperatures and a decrease in light result in the petals losing their moisture and closing.
Despite the flowers only lasting a short time, the plant itself is resilient; it thrives without much water or in poor soil.
The flowers grow on climbing vines that can reach up to three meters in a single season.
Once planted, the flowers will bloom in about one to three months.
Perhaps for the few early risers who witness this brief but unforgettable blossom, no word feels more fitting than “glorious.”

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 3 도시가 싫어서 도시를 설계한 사람
sents: Buildings are pressed up against each other and streets are crowded.
These are common sights in modern cities worldwide.
But the famed architect Frank Lloyd Wright designed an alternative called Broadacre City, with space for people to help them escape from urban environments.
Wright’s motivation was his strong dislike of densely populated, heavily industrialized cities.
He felt they limited residents’ freedom and lowered their quality of life.
So he began planning a decentralized community with the right conditions for people to live happily.
His design was revealed in the form of a massive model that was first put on display in 1935.
It shows a community of four square miles that is home to 1,400 families, each with a house on a one-acre plot of land.
There are various facilities such as farms, factories, and schools, all connected by road and rail systems.
In addition, each structure has an organic design that makes it seem part of the surrounding landscape.
Wright envisioned thousands of these communities linked together by superhighways and air transport.
Although Broadacre City was never realized, it has significantly influenced modern urban planning.
For instance, suburbs with extensive green space and public transportation are now common in many cities around the world.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 4 From Ashes to Stones
sents: When loved ones pass away, how can we remember and cherish them?
It seems there are few choices beyond visiting a cemetery or displaying an urn.
Entrepreneur Justin Crowe wanted to add another option.
After his grandfather died in 2015, he came up with the idea of turning ashes into beautiful rocks.
So in 2019, Crowe founded Parting Stone, a company that converts ashes into solid stones using a process similar to that used in making ceramics.
The ashes are first processed in a laboratory to remove any impurities, including metals from medical implants.
Then a binder is added to create a clay-like material that can be shaped into stones.
The individual pieces are hardened in a special oven, cleaned, and polished.
The finished products are not only unique in terms of shape and size, but they also vary in color.
Most are white, but some are dark green or reddish-brown.
And because they are just as hard as regular stones, they don’t break easily or dissolve in water.
Thanks to technologies like Parting Stone’s, those who have lost their loved ones can now hold a small piece of them forever.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 1 잘 맞을수록 왜 더 싫어지지...?
sents: An animated cat creeps toward a mouse.
Each slow step is accompanied by a single drumbeat.
As the cat suddenly races after the mouse, the music speeds up, matching the action on screen.
This technique of synchronizing music to on-screen action is known as “Mickey Mousing.”
The technique was popularized by Walt Disney productions in the late 1920s, though similar synchronization methods appeared in earlier animated films as well.
Filmmakers liked how it added dramatic, intense, or humorous effects that complemented the on-screen action in animated and live-action movies.
For audiences watching a film, it helped them engage with a scene.
The music guided their attention to key narrative details and to the characters’ emotional states, especially during non-verbal sequences.
However, Mickey Mousing became so overused that many filmmakers viewed it as cliché and criticized it for reducing complex emotions and narrative developments to simple, literal musical cues.

They argued that this technique undermined the depth and subtlety of storytelling, as every action and feeling is matched too obviously with the music, leaving little room for interpretation or nuance.
Accordingly, directors today prefer to use dialogue and other elements to convey characters’ emotions.
Despite this, some modern films occasionally feature this technique to add tension or comedic relief.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 2 길은 찾았는데 내 뇌는 길을 잃었네?
sents: Nowadays, when we want to go somewhere new, we simply enter the destination into a GPS device.
This process takes very little effort compared to the past, when going to an unfamiliar place meant checking a map, learning streets and landmarks, and remembering directions from others.
Although time-consuming and inconvenient, navigating without using a GPS can improve the health of our brain.
For example, the hippocampus is the region of the brain responsible for spatial memory and mental mapping, which can be developed through independent navigation.
The repeated practice of mental mapping stimulates activity in the hippocampus, which helps the brain process information more efficiently.
This was demonstrated in an observational study of aspiring London taxi drivers.
Before beginning training, each driver’s hippocampus was comparable in size to that of an average person.
They spent four years preparing for a test that required them to memorize all the streets in the city to determine the quickest route between two locations.
After training, the drivers exhibited an increase in hippocampal size.

Recently, researchers have begun studying self-guided navigation as a way to prevent cognitive diseases like Alzheimer’s, which damages tissue and causes early symptoms of disorientation and memory loss.
Since Alzheimer’s often begins by affecting the hippocampus, some scientists theorize that a larger or stronger hippocampus might offer some protection against the progression of the disease.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 3 벽을 쳐서 벽을 허무는 게임?!
sents: What do you get if you combine tennis and squash?
It’s the game of padel.
Invented in Mexico in 1969, padel is now one of the fastest-growing sports globally, played by over 25 million people across more than 100 countries!
One reason for its explosive rise in popularity is that it is incredibly exciting both to play and to watch.
As players use their padel rackets to bounce the ball against the walls and floor, the action is fast-paced and thrilling.
The ball never seems to stop moving around the tiny court!
A padel court is about three-quarters the size of a regular doubles tennis court, and it is enclosed by glass walls and metal mesh fencing.
People are also attracted to the social element of padel.
It is usually played with two players on each team, and the teammates often chat and joke with each other as well as their opponents.
Furthermore, padel clubs have developed a reputation for their laid-back, inclusive atmosphere, welcoming players regardless of their skill levels to have a good time.
If you are looking for a new sport, consider joining the world of padel.
You’re sure to make new friends while you enjoy this exciting game.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 4 A Name Worth Cutting Out
sents: How did people capture images of themselves before cameras?
One way was to visit a shadow portrait artist.
Using just scissors and paper, these artists could create incredibly accurate profile images known as silhouettes.
The term silhouette comes from the last name of Étienne de Silhouette, the finance minister of France in the 18th century.
He was notorious for his cost-cutting measures during a period of economic struggle, which led to his unpopularity.
As a result, his name became associated with things that were cheap.
His connection to the silhouette art form arose when people began creating simple, inexpensive portraits by cutting out profiles from black paper.
Soon, professional shadow portrait artists emerged, either touring Europe and America or opening their own studios in cities.
However, silhouettes were gradually replaced as photographs became more affordable.
Although they are rarely made by hand today, their distinctive style continues to appear in modern visual design.
Digital versions of silhouettes are used in the logos of major brands like the National Basketball Association, Air Jordan, and Kappa.
